facts.label: What it is
facts.text: A GLP-1 receptor agonist. It copies a gut hormone that lowers blood sugar, slows digestion, and reduces appetite. Approved for type 2 diabetes and, as Wegovy, for weight management.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Strong. Large randomised human trials (the STEP and SUSTAIN programmes).

facts.label: Common side effects
facts.text: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation. Listed warnings include pancreatitis and gallbladder problems.

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: Only with a doctor's prescription from a licensed pharmacy.

sources.title: STEP 1 trial, Wilding et al., NEJM 2021 (PubMed)

facts.label: What it is
facts.text: A dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist. It acts on two gut hormones instead of one. Approved for type 2 diabetes and weight management.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Strong. Large randomised human trials (the SURPASS and SURMOUNT programmes).

facts.label: Common side effects
facts.text: Similar to semaglutide: mainly stomach and gut effects.

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: Only with a doctor's prescription from a licensed pharmacy.

sources.title: SURMOUNT-1 trial, Jastreboff et al., NEJM 2022 (PubMed)

facts.label: What it is
facts.text: A 'triple agonist': it acts on GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors. Early trials showed large weight loss. As of September 2026 it is still investigational and not approved anywhere.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Promising but incomplete. Phase 2 published; phase 3 results still coming in.

facts.label: Safety
facts.text: Long-term safety is not yet known. Online 'retatrutide' is not the real drug — the only legitimate supply is inside clinical trials.

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: Nowhere legally, outside of an official clinical trial.

sources.title: Phase 2 trial, Jastreboff et al., NEJM 2023 (PubMed)

facts.label: What it is
facts.text: A growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) analogue. Approved in the US for one narrow use: reducing excess belly fat in people with HIV-associated lipodystrophy.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Good for its approved use. Not proven for general fat loss or muscle gain.

facts.label: Sport
facts.text: Prohibited by WADA (growth hormone releasing factors).

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: Prescription only, for its approved use.

facts.label: What it is
facts.text: A melanocortin receptor agonist. Approved in the US for low sexual desire (HSDD) in premenopausal women. Online "PT-141" vials are not the approved product.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Moderate, for its approved use (the RECONNECT trials).

facts.label: Common side effects
facts.text: Nausea, flushing, headache, temporary rise in blood pressure.

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: Prescription only, for its approved use.

facts.label: What it is
facts.text: Marketed for tendon, gut and injury healing. Most data comes from rats and lab studies. There are no large randomised human trials.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Weak in humans. Only small, uncontrolled reports.

facts.label: Regulation
facts.text: In 2023 the US FDA put it in Category 2 — substances that raise significant safety concerns for compounding (immunogenicity, impurities, too little human safety data).

facts.label: Sport
facts.text: Banned by WADA.

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: No licensed source. "Research use only" vials are unregulated and not meant for humans.

facts.label: What it is
facts.text: Marketed for recovery and tissue repair. Thymosin beta-4 has been studied in animals and in early human research for wound and eye healing, but TB-500 as sold online is not a studied medicine.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Mostly animal and lab data.

facts.label: Sport
facts.text: Prohibited by WADA.

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: No licensed source.

peptides.name: CJC-1295 & Ipamorelin
peptides.aka: Growth hormone secretagogues, often sold as a pair

facts.label: What it is
facts.text: Both push the body to release more growth hormone. CJC-1295 is a GHRH analogue; ipamorelin mimics ghrelin. Neither is approved as a medicine.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Limited. A few small early human studies; no long-term safety data.

facts.label: Sport
facts.text: Prohibited by WADA.

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: No licensed source.

facts.label: What it is
facts.text: A small copper-binding peptide found naturally in the body. Widely used in topical skincare products. Injectable versions are not an approved medicine.

facts.label: Evidence
facts.text: Some lab and small skin studies for topical use. Little human data for injection.

facts.label: Where to get it
facts.text: As an ingredient in regular cosmetic skincare.

quiz.statement: Peptides are natural, so they're safe.
quiz.explanation: Natural doesn't mean safe. Many peptides act like strong hormone signals, and untested products can be contaminated or wrongly dosed. Insulin is natural too, and the wrong dose is dangerous.

quiz.statement: Research-grade and pharma-grade peptides are the same thing.
quiz.explanation: Pharma grade is made in certified factories, tested and approved for people. "Research use only" vials aren't approved for humans, and the label may not match what's inside.

quiz.statement: Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) is an approved medicine.
quiz.explanation: It's approved for type 2 diabetes and weight management, backed by large human trials. It's prescription only, from a licensed pharmacy.

quiz.statement: BPC-157 has been proven in large human trials.
quiz.explanation: Most BPC-157 data comes from rats and lab studies. There are no large randomised human trials, and it isn't approved as a medicine anywhere.
Insulin is 51 amino acids long. It has treated diabetes for over 100 years, one of many real, well-tested peptide medicines.

quiz.statement: If it worked in rats, it will work in people.
quiz.explanation: Animal studies are only a first step. About 90% of drug candidates that reach human trials fail, mostly because they don't work well enough or aren't safe enough.

quiz.statement: Many of the peptides in this guide are banned in tested sport.
quiz.explanation: BPC-157, TB-500, CJC-1295, ipamorelin and tesamorelin are all prohibited by WADA. Tested athletes should check the WADA Prohibited List.

quiz.statement: A seller's Certificate of Analysis proves the product is pure.
quiz.explanation: Ask who did the testing. A report from the seller isn't independent, and the batch number should match the product in your hand.
